paper.title: Caffeine improves working memory in adults

paper_doc.title: Caffeine improves working memory in adults
paper_doc.authors: A. Brown and S. Kim · Department of Cognitive Science, Fake State University
paper_doc.abstract: Background: Caffeine is the most widely consumed psychoactive substance in the world, and many adults use it to stay alert while working or studying. Whether a single moderate dose changes working memory itself, rather than alertness alone, is still debated. Methods: We ran a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group trial in healthy adults who were moderate habitual caffeine consumers. Participants took placebo or one of two doses of caffeine in identical capsules and completed a visual n-back task at two memory loads, starting 45 minutes after dosing. The primary outcome was n-back accuracy. Results: Accuracy was higher after caffeine than after placebo, and the difference was clearest at the higher dose. Caffeine was well tolerated and no serious adverse events occurred. Conclusions: A single moderate dose of caffeine may support working memory performance in healthy adults. Effects at lower doses, in people who rarely consume caffeine, and with repeated daily use need further study.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Caffeine is consumed every day by a large majority of adults, mostly in coffee, tea, soft drinks and energy drinks [1, 2]. Its main action in the brain is to block adenosine receptors, which removes a signal that builds up during waking hours and promotes sleepiness [3]. Through this route caffeine raises arousal, shortens reaction times and reduces the subjective feeling of fatigue, effects that have been described in many laboratory and field studies [4, 5].
It is less clear whether caffeine improves higher cognitive functions or only makes people more alert. Working memory, the capacity to hold and update a small amount of information over a few seconds, is a natural place to look. It supports reasoning, reading comprehension and learning, and it is sensitive to changes in arousal [6, 7]. If caffeine helps people hold and manipulate information, and not only respond faster, this would matter for the many people who use it while studying or doing demanding work.
Earlier studies of caffeine and working memory have produced mixed results [8, 9]. Several used small samples, a single fixed dose, or tasks that mix memory with speed, so that faster responding could be mistaken for better remembering. Others tested participants after overnight abstinence, which makes it hard to separate a genuine benefit from the reversal of withdrawal symptoms in habitual users [10, 11]. Few studies compared more than one dose within the same design, so the shape of any dose response is poorly described [12].
The n-back task offers a well-characterised measure of working memory updating [13]. Participants watch a stream of items and indicate whether each one matches the item shown n steps earlier. Raising n increases the load on working memory while keeping the visual input the same, and accuracy at higher loads depends strongly on the ability to maintain and update the contents of memory [14]. Accuracy can be analysed separately from reaction time, which helps to tell memory effects apart from changes in speed.
We therefore designed a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial with three parallel arms: placebo and two caffeine doses. We recruited moderate habitual consumers, limited abstinence before testing to the morning of the session, and measured n-back accuracy at two memory loads. Our primary hypothesis was that caffeine would raise n-back accuracy relative to placebo, with a larger effect at the higher dose.

sections.heading: 2. Methods
sections.text: The trial was approved by the Fake State University research ethics committee and was registered before recruitment began. All participants gave written informed consent and received a small payment for their time. The protocol, materials and analysis plan were fixed before the first participant was enrolled.

sections.heading: 2.1 Participants
sections.text:
We recruited healthy adults aged 18 to 40 years through notices on campus and in the surrounding community. To be eligible, participants had to report a habitual caffeine intake of roughly one to three cups of coffee a day, or the equivalent from other sources, to have normal or corrected-to-normal vision, and to be fluent in English. We excluded people who were pregnant or breastfeeding, who smoked, who had a cardiovascular, neurological or psychiatric condition, who took medication known to interact with caffeine, or who reported a diagnosed sleep disorder. A screening call checked eligibility and recorded habitual caffeine intake with a short beverage questionnaire.
Ninety adults were randomised, 30 to each arm. Their characteristics at baseline are shown in Table 1. The arms were similar in age, sex, habitual caffeine intake, sleep on the night before testing and years of education.

table.caption: Table 1. Characteristics of participants at baseline. Values are mean (SD) unless stated otherwise.

sections.heading: 2.2 Design and randomisation
sections.text: The trial used a parallel-group design with three arms: placebo, 100 mg caffeine and 200 mg caffeine. A researcher who had no contact with participants generated the allocation sequence by computer in permuted blocks of six and prepared numbered, sealed packs of capsules. Participants, the researchers who ran the sessions and the researcher who scored the task were all unaware of the allocation until the database was locked. The flow of participants through the trial is shown in Figure 1.

figure.caption: Figure 1. Flow of participants through the trial, from screening and randomisation to analysis.

sections.heading: 2.3 Intervention
sections.text: Capsules were identical in size, colour and weight. Active capsules contained 100 mg or 200 mg of anhydrous caffeine with a cellulose filler, and placebo capsules contained the filler alone. A pharmacist outside the research team filled and labelled the capsules. Participants were asked to avoid caffeine from waking on the day of testing, to eat a light breakfast and to avoid alcohol on the evening before. Compliance with these requests was checked with a short questionnaire on arrival.

sections.heading: 2.4 Working memory task
sections.text: Working memory was measured with a visual letter n-back task presented on a laptop computer. Letters appeared one at a time in the centre of the screen for 500 ms, followed by a blank interval of 2000 ms. Participants pressed one key when the current letter matched the letter shown n positions earlier and another key when it did not. Each session included blocks at the 2-back and 3-back loads, presented in a counterbalanced order, with one third of the trials being targets. Accuracy was defined as the proportion of correct responses across targets and non-targets. Reaction time on correct trials was recorded as a secondary measure. Before the main task, participants completed a short practice at the 1-back and 2-back loads until they understood the instructions.

sections.heading: 2.5 Procedure
sections.text: Sessions took place between 9 and 11 in the morning in a quiet testing room. After arrival, participants completed the compliance questionnaire, a rating of current alertness and the practice blocks. They then swallowed the capsule with water and rested for 45 minutes, during which they could read material that we provided but not use their phones. The main n-back task began 45 minutes after dosing and lasted about 25 minutes, divided into four blocks with short breaks between them. At the end of the session participants rated their alertness again, reported any side effects on a checklist and guessed whether they had received caffeine or placebo.

sections.heading: 2.6 Statistical analysis
sections.text: The sample size was chosen to detect a moderate difference in accuracy between each caffeine arm and placebo with 80% power at a two-sided alpha of 0.05. The primary analysis compared n-back accuracy between arms with an analysis of covariance that adjusted for habitual caffeine intake and for accuracy in the practice blocks. Each caffeine arm was compared with placebo. Memory load was included as a within-participant factor in a secondary model. Reaction time and alertness ratings were analysed in the same way. All randomised participants who completed the task were included in the analysis in the arm to which they were allocated. Analyses were carried out with standard statistical software by a researcher who was unaware of allocation.

sections.heading: 3. Results
sections.text: Recruitment ran over five months. All 90 randomised participants attended their session, took the capsule and completed the n-back task, so no data were missing for the primary outcome. Self-reported compliance with the caffeine and alcohol restrictions was high and similar across arms.

sections.heading: 3.1 Blinding
sections.text: At the end of the session, participants guessed which capsule they had received. The proportion of correct guesses did not differ clearly from what would be expected by chance in any arm, which suggests that blinding was largely maintained. Participants in the caffeine arms rated themselves as somewhat more alert after the task than those given placebo.

sections.heading: 3.2 Working memory accuracy
sections.text: In this double-blind trial of 90 adults, 200 mg caffeine improved n-back accuracy by 12% compared with placebo. Figures 2 to 4 show accuracy by dose. The improvement was significant at 200 mg (p = 0.01). The pattern was similar at both memory loads, and accuracy stayed stable across the four task blocks in each arm.

figure.caption: Figure 2. Mean n-back accuracy by dose across both memory loads. Error bars show 95% confidence intervals.

sections.text: Figures 3 and 4 break the same accuracy data down by memory load and by task block.

figure.caption: Figure 3. Mean n-back accuracy by dose, shown separately for the 2-back and 3-back loads.
Figure 4. Mean n-back accuracy by dose in each of the four task blocks, from the first block to the last.

sections.heading: 3.3 Reaction time and alertness
sections.text: Reaction times on correct trials and the alertness ratings are reported in the supplementary material. The main analyses of these secondary measures followed the same model as the primary analysis.

sections.heading: 3.4 Tolerability
sections.text: Caffeine was well tolerated. The side effects reported on the checklist are shown in Table 2. Most were mild and had resolved by the end of the session. No participant withdrew because of side effects and no serious adverse events occurred.

table.caption: Table 2. Participants reporting each side effect at the end of the session, n.

sections.heading: 4. Discussion
sections.text:
In this trial, healthy adults who were moderate habitual caffeine consumers performed a visual n-back task more accurately after taking caffeine than after taking placebo. The effect was most evident at the higher of the two doses we tested, and caffeine was well tolerated at both doses.
Because we analysed accuracy rather than speed, the benefit is unlikely to reflect faster responding alone. The n-back task requires participants to keep a short sequence of items in mind and to update it continuously, and our findings suggest that caffeine may support this process. One possible explanation is that caffeine, by blocking adenosine receptors, increases the release of neurotransmitters in frontal and parietal regions that support working memory [15, 16]. Another is that caffeine sustains attention over the course of a demanding task, so that fewer items are lost through lapses [17].
Our design addressed several limitations of earlier work. We tested more than one dose, randomised participants to parallel arms so that practice effects could not differ between conditions, and restricted abstinence to the morning of testing. Withdrawal after a short morning abstinence is usually mild, but we cannot exclude that part of the difference from placebo reflects the relief of mild withdrawal symptoms in habitual consumers, a question that has been debated for many years [10, 18].
The findings fit with reports that caffeine improves performance on tasks that demand sustained attention and with neuroimaging studies that link caffeine to changes in activity in working memory networks [19, 20]. They also suggest that the doses commonly found in one or two cups of coffee are enough to produce a measurable effect in a laboratory setting. Whether such effects carry over to real study or work, where many other factors influence performance, is an open question.

sections.heading: 4.1 Limitations
sections.text: This study has several limitations. Participants were young, healthy and mostly university students or staff, so the results may not apply to older adults, to people with medical conditions, or to people who rarely consume caffeine. We tested a single session, so we cannot say whether the effect persists with repeated daily use, when tolerance may develop [21]. The n-back task measures one aspect of working memory, and other tasks might show a different pattern. Finally, although the blinding check suggested that most participants could not tell which capsule they had received, those given caffeine felt more alert, and expectations may have influenced performance [22].

sections.heading: 5. Conclusion
sections.text: A single moderate dose of caffeine may support working memory performance in healthy adults who are habitual consumers. Further trials should test a wider range of doses, include people who rarely consume caffeine, and follow participants over repeated use and in real-world settings such as study and work.

sections.heading: Acknowledgements, funding and data
sections.text: We thank the participants and the staff of the testing laboratory. The study was funded by an internal research grant from Fake State University, which had no role in the design, conduct or reporting of the trial. The authors declare no competing interests. The data are available from the corresponding author on reasonable request.

alerts.description: A retraction notice was published for this paper.

notice.text:
Retraction: Caffeine improves working memory in adults

The journal has retracted this article. An institutional investigation found that the data in Figures 2 to 4 had been fabricated, and the conclusions cannot be relied on. The authors have not responded.

draft_doc.title: Caffeine and study performance
draft_doc.authors: J. Lee, M. Ortiz and P. Nair · School of Education, Fake City University
draft_doc.abstract: Coffee and energy drinks are a common companion to studying at university, and students often hope that caffeine will help them learn. Laboratory work on caffeine has mostly relied on abstract tasks, so we know little about whether a dose taken before studying changes how well students take in, and later recall, real course material. This manuscript sets out a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled experiment with undergraduates. Each participant takes a capsule containing caffeine or placebo, studies a passage from an introductory course for 30 minutes, and sits a recall and comprehension test at the end of the session and once more two days later. Self-rated alertness, anxiety and sleep on the following night are also recorded. We present the design, the planned analyses, the limitations we anticipate and the reasons for the study, and we explain how the findings could shape the advice students receive about caffeine during exam periods.

sections.heading: 1. Methods
sections.text:
Design. The study is a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled experiment with two parallel groups. An administrator who has no contact with participants will generate the allocation list by computer and prepare numbered capsule packs.
Participants. We plan to recruit 120 undergraduate students aged 18 to 30 through course announcements and the department's participant pool. Students must report drinking at least one caffeinated drink on most days, must not have taken the introductory economics course from which the study passage is taken, and must be fluent in English. We will exclude students who are pregnant, who have a heart condition, anxiety disorder or sleep disorder, or who take medication that interacts with caffeine. Habitual caffeine intake will be recorded with a beverage questionnaire at screening.
Intervention. Participants received 200 mg caffeine or placebo. Capsules are identical in appearance and are prepared by a pharmacy outside the research team. Participants are asked to avoid caffeine from waking on the day of the session and to keep to their usual sleep schedule the night before.
Materials. The study passage is a 2,400-word chapter on supply and demand from an introductory economics textbook, adapted with permission and checked by two instructors for accuracy and difficulty. The test has 20 free-recall prompts and 20 multiple-choice comprehension questions, written by the instructors and piloted with students who did not take part in the main study. Two parallel forms of the test are used for the immediate and delayed sessions, in counterbalanced order.
Procedure. Sessions begin at 2 pm. After consent, participants rate their alertness and anxiety, take the capsule, and rest for 40 minutes. They then study the passage for 30 minutes and may take notes, which are collected before testing. After a 10-minute break they complete the immediate test. Participants wear a wrist actigraphy device on the following night and return two days later, at the same time of day, for the delayed test. The session schedule is shown in Table 1.

table.caption: Table 1. Schedule of the study session and the delayed test.

sections.heading: 2. Introduction
sections.text:
For many students, caffeine is a daily habit. Surveys carried out at universities in several countries report that most students consume it regularly, and that consumption climbs during exam periods, when coffee, energy drinks and caffeine tablets help them study for longer and get by on less sleep [1, 2]. Students often believe that caffeine sharpens their concentration and helps them remember what they have read, a belief that some university advice pages pass on [4]. Evidence that caffeine helps students learn real course material, as opposed to performing short laboratory tasks, is nevertheless scarce.
How caffeine acts on the brain is well established. By blocking adenosine receptors, it slows the build-up of sleep pressure across the day and raises arousal [5]. In the laboratory, moderate doses speed up reaction times, sharpen vigilance and lessen the feeling of fatigue, above all in people who are tired or have had a poor night [6, 7]. Students, who often study late at night or after short sleep, are exactly the people for whom these effects matter.
Staying awake, though, is only part of learning from a textbook or a lecture. A student has to attend to new information, keep it in mind while linking it to existing knowledge, and store it so that it can be retrieved days or weeks afterwards. The first two steps lean heavily on working memory, and people with greater working memory capacity tend to do better at reading comprehension and in exams [8, 9]. Retaining material over the long term also relies on consolidation, which carries on after studying ends and is sensitive to sleep [10].
Two questions follow. Does caffeine taken before a study session help students encode course material, perhaps by improving attention and working memory while they study? And does any such benefit last until a delayed test, or is it cancelled out if caffeine disturbs sleep the next night? Research with abstract materials has not settled whether caffeine helps memory, and few studies have used meaningful material with a delay longer than a few hours [11, 12]. Afternoon or evening caffeine can push back sleep onset and cut deep sleep, which may weaken consolidation [13].
Sleep deserves special attention in students. During term, many say they sleep less than they need, stay up later before deadlines and make up for it at weekends, so they are often tired just when they most want to study [7]. Students who lack sleep may benefit more from caffeine while studying than rested students do, yet they may also be more inclined to take it late in the day, when it is most likely to postpone sleep that night. A full account of caffeine and student learning must therefore look at the hours after a study session as well as the session itself.
Much of what we know also comes from settings unlike real studying. In the laboratory, participants typically do brief computerised tasks shortly after dosing and have no stake in the result, whereas students work on material they will be examined on, for longer stretches, with breaks, distractions and their own note-taking strategies [11, 12]. Classroom and field studies of stimulant use do exist, but most are observational, depend on self-reported intake and grades, and cannot disentangle the effect of caffeine from the habits of its heaviest users [2, 22]. An experiment that combines real course material with the control of a laboratory study would help close this gap.
How learning is measured also matters. A test taken straight after study mainly reflects what was encoded and what is still in short-term memory, whereas a test taken days later also reflects consolidation and forgetting [10]. Free recall is sensitive to how well the material was organised while studying, and comprehension questions show whether students grasped how ideas relate rather than isolated facts. Prior achievement strongly predicts both kinds of score and should be allowed for when groups are compared [17]. We therefore use free recall and comprehension at both an immediate and a delayed test.
Both questions depend on the dose. A low dose may do too little to change performance in rested participants, whereas a high dose raises the risk of anxiety, jitteriness and poor sleep, any of which could get in the way of learning [14, 15]. Many students rely on caffeine. We set our dose at 200 mg because Brown and Kim [3] reported that this amount raises working memory performance by 12%. That is about what two cups of brewed coffee contain, and it lies within the range food safety agencies consider safe as a single serving for healthy adults [16].
We therefore test whether 200 mg of caffeine, taken before a study session, improves undergraduates' immediate and delayed recall and comprehension of course material relative to placebo. We also look at whether caffeine alters self-rated alertness and anxiety during the session and sleep the following night, and whether any such changes are linked to how much students learn.

sections.heading: 3. Planned analysis
sections.text: The primary outcome is the delayed test score, the sum of free-recall and comprehension points two days after the session. Secondary outcomes are the immediate test score, alertness and anxiety ratings, and total sleep time and sleep onset latency on the following night. The groups will be compared with linear models that adjust for habitual caffeine intake and for prior grade point average, which is a strong predictor of test performance [17]. A mediation analysis will examine whether sleep on the following night explains any difference between the immediate and delayed effects of caffeine [18]. With 60 students per group, the study has 80% power to detect a moderate group difference at a two-sided alpha of 0.05. The analysis plan will be registered before data collection begins, and all deviations from it will be reported.

sections.heading: 4. Expected limitations
sections.text: Several limitations are expected. The study tests a single session and a single passage, and real exam preparation involves repeated study over weeks, often with repeated caffeine use and the tolerance that comes with it [19]. Participants are habitual consumers who abstain on the morning of the session, so part of any difference from placebo may reflect relief from mild withdrawal [20]. Blinding may be imperfect, since some participants will notice the effects of caffeine, and expectations about caffeine can themselves change performance [21]. Finally, students who volunteer for a study about caffeine may differ from the wider student population in their caffeine use and study habits. We will record participants' guesses about their group to assess blinding, and we will compare the sample with campus survey data on caffeine use [22].

sections.heading: 5. Ethics and data management
sections.text: The study has been submitted to the Fake City University ethics committee. Participants will receive course credit or a small payment and may withdraw at any time without giving a reason. Data will be stored on a secure university server under study codes, and the anonymised dataset and analysis code will be shared in a public repository when the study is published.
